content:
If I use macro to generate a theorem, Visual Studio Code shows a checkmark if the theorem is proven:

macro "foo" : command =>
  `(example: 0 = 0 := by trivial)

foo    -- checkmark appears in left column

But if I use elab, there is no checkmark:

import Lean
open Lean.Elab.Command

elab "bar" : command => do
  let c ← `(example: 0 = 0 := by trivial)
  elabCommand c

bar   -- no checkmark

I'm generating a theorem programmatically, and am using elab since I need access to CoreM for various reasons. Is there any way to get a checkmark for a theorem generated in this way? Alternatively, is there some way to get access to CoreM inside a macro definition?

I studied the Lean source code and ran some experiments to learn more about what's going on here.

The function logGoalsAccomplishedSnapshotTask in Lean/Elab/MutualDef.lean logs a goalsAccomplished message for each theorem if it has no errors or sorrys . This message causes VS Code to display a double checkmark beside each such theorem.

This function takes a couple of arguments including defParsedSnap: DefsParsedSnapshot which holds a snapshot of the syntax tree and some other information. However in my second example above, where the command elaborator generates the theorem, defsParsedSnap.defsis empty, because the calling function Lean.Elab.Command.elabMutualDef didn't add anything to it. That in turn is because (← read).snap? is none, i.e. no snapshot is available. I think this is related to the difference between incremental macros and incremental command elaboration as described in the long comment block at the top of Language/Lean.lean.

Now, logGoalsAccomplishedSnapshotTask needs the argument defParsedSnap: DefsParsedSnapshot only for one purpose: to determine whether an example has type Prop or not. That's because we don't want to display a checkmark beside an example such as

example: Int := 5

though I believe that non-Prop examples should be pretty rare.

Thus, one easy fix is to simply remove the defParseSnap argument, and assume that all examples are Props. Then we won't try to iterate over defParseSnap, and will get check marks for all theorems including those generated in an elab. I tried this in a custom Lean build and it worked fine. However, this means that any non-Prop example (even one at top level, outside a macro or elab) will get a check mark.

Alternatively, we could keep defParseSnap, but if it doesn't contain any definitions (which will happen if a theorem or example was generated in an elab) then we won't be able to check whether an example is a Prop, so we'll always display a check mark by it. Maybe not ideal, but that should now be a super rare edge case (i.e. a non-Prop example that was generated by an elab).

I'm happy to make a pull request for either of these approaches. Thoughts?
I just created an issue for this behavior and a pull request that fixes it, so any further discussion can happen there.
